THREAT INTELLIGENCE NOTE   Source: managed detection provider   Received: 2026-04-05

Subject: Credential exposure affecting Meridian Cold Chain domain

Our monitoring of criminal marketplaces identified a combolist posted on 2026-03-31 containing
credential pairs for several meridiancoldchain.com addresses. One pair is for leila.okafor@meridiancoldchain.com. The password
in the dump matches the pattern of a previously used corporate password for this user
(hash comparison performed with the client's identity team, see ticket HD-42507).

Password age check (2026-04-06): the current password for ACC-5712 was last changed 371 days
ago, i.e. BEFORE the dump was posted. The exposed credential is therefore believed to be
current.

Recommendation: force password reset and MFA enrolment for ACC-5712; review legacy
protocol access (IMAP/POP) which bypasses MFA in this tenant.

The same combolist contained no other meridiancoldchain.com addresses.
</document>

steps.reasoning_summary: I'm guessing Priya's note is about a travel authorization, so I'll quickly check DOC-013 and DOC-008 and flag them as benign if they hold up. Her sign-in is fine. Leila's case is different: a sign-in from an unfamiliar device using exposed credentials that succeeded, so I'm treating that account as compromised and submitting it.

args.reasoning:
Three accounts are compromised.

ACC-4329 (Marcus Raman):
- DOC-003: a sign-in from Lagos (144.236.201.214, unmanaged Linux) came 40 minutes after an Antwerp sign-in on a managed laptop. The risk engine flagged atypical travel.
- DOC-032: an inbox rule named "." was created from the Lagos IP. It forwards all mail to an external protonmail address and deletes the originals.
- DOC-011: a fraudulent Kestrel Fleet Leasing bank-detail change (WR-3317) was submitted from the same Lagos IP. It is pending second approval.

ACC-9965 (Mei Chen):
- DOC-010: 11 MFA push prompts from the same Lagos IP came in the early hours (03:06–03:16 UTC). The user eventually approved one, which is MFA fatigue.
- DOC-024: Mei Chen confirms she did not initiate the prompts and approved one to make them stop.
- DOC-007: right after the approval, an unverified "MailSync Pro" app was granted Mail.ReadWrite and Mail.Send with offline_access. The grant came from the Lagos IP.

ACC-5712 (Leila Okafor):
- DOC-006 and DOC-017: her credential appeared in a leaked combolist. Her password was last changed 371 days ago, before the dump, so the exposed password is still current.
- DOC-003: a password-only sign-in succeeded on 2026-04-07 from an unfamiliar device and network in Sao Paulo. It used legacy IMAP, which bypasses MFA. The user was out of office, and the reset had not been done.

Reviewed and judged benign:
- ACC-8290 (Priya Moreau): Toronto sign-ins came from the managed CFO laptop over the corporate VPN, with MFA approvals (DOC-003, DOC-010).
- ACC-2501 (Lucia Novak): the failed logins came from her own managed laptop. The password was reset after in-person verification (DOC-009).
- ACC-4012 (Viktor Ivanova): the "Newsletters" inbox rule was created from the internal warehouse terminal and is benign (DOC-032).
- ACC-7306 (Chloe Berg): the Zoom admin consent is a verified publisher app, granted from the internal network (DOC-007).
- ACC-5756 (Aisha Marinescu): her activity came from an internal Antwerp session and looks routine (DOC-011).

I'm marking ACC-7014, ACC-9991, and ACC-7139 as compromised, since the sign-ins from Brazil used exposed credentials. The timestamp is in UTC+2 and the login prompts fall at 03:06 UTC, which I'll account for. Mei's Gothenburg sign-in at 08:20 looks fine, and ACC-9535 for Lucia checks out as legitimate.

ACC-7014 (Marcus Holm): DOC-032 shows a Gothenburg sign-in at 08:12 UTC. At 08:52 UTC there was a sign-in from Lagos (156.121.167.99) on an unmanaged Linux device, flagged as atypical travel. steps.reasoning_summary:
I'm tracing ACC-4238, an MFA fatigue attack where the approval landed at 03:16. The timestamps don't line up cleanly: the note gives a UTC+1 clock, and the OAuth consent at 03:14 precedes that approval, but both come from the same Manila IP. Leila's sign-in in Hamburg at 08:20 is what I'm weighing against that, and the malicious OAuth app makes this a compromise.

Rafael's case also shows a Manila IP, a mailbox rule, and a bank detail change. ACC-6059 looks like a Jakarta legacy login tied to a phishing email from a lookalike domain, and Aisha's Dubai session is managed and benign, so that one's done.

steps.reasoning_summary: I've flagged three accounts as compromised: ACC-9179, ACC-3358, and ACC-1372. Rafael Haugen, the CFO in Barcelona, looks benign based on DOC-004 and DOC-012, so that's a quick call.

args.reasoning:
Three accounts are compromised.

ACC-9179 (Nadia Castillo):
- DOC-018: a sign-in from Manila (155.2.105.220) on an unmanaged Linux device, 40 minutes after an Antwerp sign-in on her managed laptop. The Manila sign-in used password plus SMS code.
- DOC-032: at 09:04 UTC, a session from the same Manila IP created a mailbox rule named "." that forwards all mail to an external ProtonMail address, marks it read and moves it to Deleted Items.
- DOC-019: at 09:21 UTC, a session from the same IP submitted bank change request WR-3914 for Blue Meridian Insurance. It moves the IBAN to a Riga bank and claims "CFO approved by phone". This is payment-fraud activity.

ACC-3358 (Kwame Ivanova):
- DOC-023 and DOC-013: his credential appeared in a leaked combolist, and the password was not changed after the dump. Legacy IMAP bypasses MFA, and the account was still unreset.
- DOC-018: a password-only sign-in from an unfamiliar device and network in Sao Paulo at 02:58 UTC on 11-13. He was out of office, and the account had been flagged.

ACC-1372 (Oscar Moreau):
- DOC-026: an MFA fatigue attack. Eleven prompts came from Manila (the same attacker IP, 155.2.105.220), and the last was approved at 03:16 UTC.
- DOC-024: Oscar confirms he approved one prompt just to make them stop.
- DOC-029: at 03:14 UTC, from the Manila IP, an unverified app "MailSync Pro" was granted Mail.ReadWrite, Mail.Send and offline_access. This gives the attacker persistent mailbox access.

Ruled out as benign:
- ACC-4805 (Rafael Haugen): the Barcelona sign-ins came from a managed laptop over the corporate VPN and match his travel (DOC-004, DOC-012).
- ACC-7655 (Aisha Petrova): the failed logins were followed by a verified admin reset, ticket HD-40463.
- ACC-7553 (Felix Marinescu): the "Newsletters" mailbox rule was created from an internal IP and is harmless.
- ACC-7049 (Daniel Holm): the Zoom admin consent is a verified publisher and came from an internal IP.
